sardine.distribution: Northeast Atlantic, Mediterranean and Black Sea coasts, mostly in near-shore mid-to-surface waters
sardine.behavior: Migrates in huge schools of thousands; rises at night and sinks by day
facts: Many of the “sardines” in European tins are this species
Its vast schools feed tuna, dolphins and seabirds

mackerel.distribution: Temperate and subtropical Indo-Pacific coasts; common along China's coast
mackerel.behavior: Fast-swimming schooling fish; juveniles stay near beaches and seaweed beds, adults over deeper banks; can live about 18 years
mackerel.season: Comes inshore in spring and autumn
facts: The dark wavy lines on its back give it its Chinese name “blue-patterned fish”
Rich in omega-3, but forms histamine quickly if not kept fresh

crab.distribution: Shallow sandy-muddy seabeds off China, Japan and Korea
crab.diet: Small fish, shellfish, worms and carrion
crab.behavior: Its last pair of legs are flattened like paddles for swimming; often buries itself in sand by day
facts: Three wart-like bumps on its shell give it its Chinese name
One of China's most-landed marine crabs

seabream.size: Usually 30–70 cm; up to about 1.2 m
seabream.distribution: Northwest Pacific: coasts of China, Japan and Korea
seabream.diet: Bottom crustaceans, shellfish and small fish
seabream.behavior: Adults live alone over reefs 30–200 m deep; typically live 20–40 years
facts: A symbol of celebration and good luck in Japan
Bright red with small blue spots

mudskipper.distribution: Mudflats, estuaries and mangroves of the Northwest Pacific coast
mudskipper.behavior: “Walks” and hops across mud on its pectoral fins, breathing through moist skin and mouth
facts: One of the few fish that can stay out of water for long periods
Its eyes sit on top of its head like periscopes

tigerprawn.size: Females up to about 33 cm (usually 25–30 cm); males slightly smaller
tigerprawn.distribution: Coasts, estuaries and mangroves of the Indo-West Pacific
tigerprawn.diet: Algal detritus and small bottom animals
tigerprawn.behavior: Larvae grow up in sandy estuaries and mangroves; adults move to deeper (0–110 m) muddy or rocky seabeds
facts: One of the world's most important farmed shrimps
Its dark and light bands look like tiger stripes

mudcrab.size: Carapace up to about 26 cm wide; up to about 3.5 kg
mudcrab.distribution: Mangroves and estuarine mudflats of the Indo-West Pacific
mudcrab.diet: Shellfish, crustaceans, small fish and carrion
mudcrab.behavior: Digs burrows in the mud; its claws are very powerful
facts: Mature females full of roe are prized in Chinese cuisine
Its Chinese name refers to the saw-toothed edge of its shell

barramundi.size: Usually under 1 m; can reach 1.8 m (rarely recorded)
barramundi.distribution: Indo-West Pacific, from the Persian Gulf to northern Australia: coasts, estuaries and rivers
barramundi.behavior: Migrates between fresh and salt water; many start life male and become female as they grow
facts: Its male-to-female sex change is famous
A prized sport fish in Australia

clown.distribution: Coral reefs of the eastern Indian Ocean and western Pacific
clown.behavior: Lives with sea anemones; a mucus coat protects it from their stings
facts: The largest fish in a group is female; if she dies, the biggest male becomes female
Nemo from Finding Nemo is this species

squid.distribution: Coral reefs and seagrass beds of the Indo-West Pacific
squid.behavior: Changes colour and pattern in an instant to hide and communicate; often schools in shallow water
facts: Short-lived, usually under a year
Its fins run almost the full length of its body and ripple as it swims

lobster.size: A large lobster; farmed ones reach 1 kg in about 18 months
lobster.distribution: Indo-West Pacific, usually on reefs shallower than 50 m
lobster.diet: Shellfish, sea urchins and other bottom invertebrates
lobster.behavior: Matures after 1–2 years on the reef and makes a yearly mass migration to breed
facts: A “spiny lobster” with no big claws
Its shell is ornately patterned in blue-green, yellow and black

coraltrout.aliases: leopard coral trout, spotted coral grouper
coraltrout.size: Usually about 35 cm; max about 1.2 m and 23.6 kg
coraltrout.distribution: Western Pacific coral reefs, 3–100 m deep
coraltrout.behavior: An ambush predator; starts female and turns male at about 42 cm on average
facts: A luxury live seafood in Hong Kong and southern China
Covered in small blue spots like a leopard

urchin.distribution: Pacific coast of North America (Alaska to Mexico), intertidal zones and kelp forests
urchin.behavior: Moves slowly on tube feet and spines; population booms can strip kelp forests into “urchin barrens”
facts: Sea otters love to eat it, so kelp grows thicker where otters are common
A model organism in developmental biology; its genome was sequenced in 2006

abalone.size: A medium-to-large abalone (exact size not verified)
abalone.distribution: Northwest Pacific: Korea, northeast Honshu and western Hokkaido; farmed in northern China
abalone.diet: Kelp, wakame and other brown algae
abalone.behavior: Lives on wave-swept rocky shores 1–5 m deep, clinging to rock with its strong foot
facts: A row of small holes along its shell lets out water for breathing
The photo shows the nominate subspecies Haliotis discus discus

yellowtail.size: Usually about 1 m; max about 1.5 m
yellowtail.distribution: Northwest Pacific: coasts of Japan, Korea and China
yellowtail.behavior: A fast, open-water fish with a yellow stripe along its body and a yellow tail
facts: Japan has different names for it at each size — a “promotion fish”
Hamachi in Japanese cuisine usually means this fish

seadragon.distribution: Only southern and western Australian coasts, around weedy rocks and seagrass within 50 m depth
seadragon.diet: Mysid shrimp and other tiny crustaceans
seadragon.behavior: Covered in leaf-like flaps that look like drifting seaweed; the male carries the eggs on his tail
facts: The marine emblem of South Australia
Its leafy flaps are only for camouflage, not swimming

tuna.size: Recorded up to about 2.4 m and 200 kg
tuna.distribution: Tropical and subtropical open oceans worldwide
tuna.behavior: Extremely fast; often travels with dolphin pods or under floating objects
facts: Its second dorsal and anal fins are bright yellow
A major source of canned tuna

mahimahi.distribution: Surface waters of tropical and subtropical seas worldwide
mahimahi.diet: Flying fish, small fish and squid
mahimahi.behavior: An open-ocean surface fish that gathers around floating debris; can spawn at only about 20 cm
facts: Males have a tall, blunt forehead
Golden sides with brilliant blue and green on the back

puffer.size: A medium-to-large puffer (often cited at 70–80 cm max; not fully verified)
puffer.distribution: Northwest Pacific: Yellow Sea, East China Sea and Japanese coasts
puffer.behavior: Inflates by gulping water when alarmed; its organs contain tetrodotoxin
facts: Some organs hold deadly tetrodotoxin (TTX); chefs in Japan need a special licence to prepare it
Its teeth are fused into a hard “beak” that crushes shells

swordfish.behavior: Slashes at schools of fish with its flat bill; dives deep by day and rises at night
facts: A special heater organ warms its eyes and brain 10–15 °C above the water for sharper vision
Adults lose all their teeth and scales

cod.size: Usually about 1 m; up to 2 m
cod.distribution: Cold continental shelves on both sides of the North Atlantic
cod.behavior: Uses a chin barbel to feel for food on the seabed
facts: Canada closed its cod fishery in 1992 after a collapse; stocks have still not fully recovered
The classic fish in British fish and chips

salmon.distribution: North Atlantic and the rivers that flow into it
salmon.diet: Fish and crustaceans at sea; insects as juveniles
salmon.behavior: Born in rivers, grows up at sea, and returns to its home river to spawn
facts: Can leap waterfalls several metres high
Unlike Pacific salmon, some survive spawning and return again

charr.distribution: Arctic and subarctic lakes, rivers and coasts
charr.behavior: Some populations migrate to sea, others stay in fresh water; the belly turns bright red when breeding
facts: One of the most northerly freshwater fish
Thrives in water close to 0 °C

kingcrab.size: Leg span up to about 1.8 m, carapace about 28 cm, weight up to about 12.7 kg
kingcrab.distribution: North Pacific (Bering and Okhotsk Seas); introduced to the Barents Sea
kingcrab.diet: Shellfish, sea urchins, worms and more
kingcrab.behavior: Lives in cold water of about −1.8 to 12.8 °C and migrates seasonally
facts: Strictly speaking it is closer to hermit crabs than to true crabs
It seems to have 8 legs; the tiny fifth pair is tucked under its shell

monkfish.size: A large bottom-dwelling fish (maximum size not verified)
monkfish.distribution: Northwest Pacific: muddy and sandy bottoms of the Yellow Sea, East China Sea and off Japan
monkfish.behavior: Lies on the seabed and lures prey with a “fishing rod” grown from its dorsal fin
facts: Its huge mouth can swallow prey nearly its own size
Its liver is a delicacy known as “the foie gras of the sea”

octopus.size: Adults usually about 15 kg, arm span up to about 4.3 m
octopus.distribution: North Pacific, from the intertidal zone to about 2,000 m in cold water
octopus.behavior: Very intelligent — can open jars and solve mazes; the female guards her eggs until they hatch, then dies
facts: One of the largest octopuses; its biggest suckers are about 6.4 cm across
Like other octopuses it has three hearts and blue blood

giantsquid.size: Females estimated at 12–13 m total length, males about 10 m
giantsquid.behavior: Rarely seen alive; first photographed in the wild in 2004
facts: Its eyes are at least 27 cm across — among the largest of any living animal
A Japanese team took the first photos of a live one in the wild in 2004

oarfish.size: Recorded at 7–8 m (possibly 11 m) — the longest bony fish in the world
oarfish.distribution: Mid-depth waters of temperate to tropical seas worldwide
oarfish.behavior: Hangs vertically in the water and swims by rippling its dorsal fin
facts: Nicknamed the “earthquake fish”, but there is no scientific evidence it predicts quakes
Thought to be one source of sea-serpent legends

bluefin.size: Mature fish average about 2–2.5 m and 225–250 kg
bluefin.behavior: A warm-blooded fish that migrates across the Atlantic
facts: One of the most expensive food fish
In 2021 the IUCN moved it from Endangered to Least Concern thanks to fishery management

sunfish.behavior: Sometimes lies flat at the surface so seabirds can pick off parasites; spends most time feeding deeper
facts: One of the heaviest bony fish
Feeds mainly on jellyfish and other gelatinous plankton

megamouth.distribution: Tropical and temperate seas worldwide; rare
megamouth.behavior: A filter feeder that stays deep by day and rises at night following plankton
facts: First discovered near Hawaii in 1976
As of March 2025, only about 296 captures or sightings had been recorded

coelacanth.distribution: Western Indian Ocean: deep water off South Africa, Comoros, Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique and Madagascar
coelacanth.behavior: Hides in seabed caves by day and feeds slowly at night; moves its fleshy fins alternately like limbs
facts: Thought extinct since the age of dinosaurs until rediscovered off South Africa's Chalumna River in December 1938
Studies suggest it may live about 100 years

greenlandshark.size: Adults about 4–5 m; max confirmed length about 6.4 m
greenlandshark.distribution: Cold, deep waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans
greenlandshark.behavior: One of the slowest-swimming fish in the world, cruising through near-freezing water
facts: The longest-lived vertebrate known, estimated at 272–510 years
Its metabolism is so slow it is thought to grow only about 1 cm a year

polarcod.size: Average about 25 cm; max about 40 cm
polarcod.distribution: The Arctic Ocean and nearby cold seas, often under sea ice
polarcod.behavior: Hides in cracks in the sea ice; a keystone of the Arctic food web
facts: Antifreeze glycoproteins in its blood keep it from freezing below 0 °C
Seals, belugas and seabirds depend on it

halibut.size: Usually 80–100 cm; max about 1.2 m and 45 kg
halibut.distribution: Cold deep waters of the North Atlantic, North Pacific and Arctic, mostly 500–1,000 m
halibut.behavior: A flatfish that often leaves the bottom to hunt in mid-water
facts: As it grows, its left eye migrates to the right side of its head
It is the only species in its genus, Reinhardtius

snowcrab.size: Carapace about as long as it is wide, with long slender legs
snowcrab.distribution: Cold continental shelves of the northwest Atlantic and North Pacific
snowcrab.behavior: Lives on muddy-sandy shelf bottoms in cold water; caught with traps or trawls
facts: In Japan it is the prized winter crab “matsuba-gani”
Prefers very cold water of around 0–2 °C

krill.size: Up to about 6 cm long and 2 g
krill.behavior: Forms vast swarms of 10,000–30,000 animals per cubic metre; can live about 6 years
facts: Its total biomass is about 500 million tonnes — one of the most abundant animals on Earth
The staple food of whales, penguins, seals and seabirds

toothfish.size: Up to about 1.7 m and 135 kg
toothfish.distribution: Frigid waters of the Southern Ocean around Antarctica
toothfish.behavior: The largest bony fish of the Southern Ocean; has antifreeze proteins and grows slowly
facts: Sold as “Chilean sea bass” along with its sister species, the Patagonian toothfish
Preyed on by orcas and seals

icefish.size: Max about 66 cm; usually about 35 cm
icefish.distribution: Southern Ocean and the far South Atlantic, around South Georgia, Kerguelen and other islands, 0–700 m
icefish.behavior: Lives in near-freezing water, usually 30–250 m deep
facts: Icefishes have no haemoglobin — their blood is almost clear
They survive thanks to oxygen-rich polar water and a large heart
